title: Anaemia in pregnancy (BSH, WHO and ACOG)
subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
setting: Antenatal clinic, day unit, labour ward, postnatal
summary: Anaemia in pregnancy is haemoglobin below 110 g/L in the first trimester and below 105 g/L later (BSH). Give all women daily iron and folic acid (WHO), treat iron deficiency with 40 to 80 mg elemental iron daily or on alternate days, recheck Hb at 2 to 3 weeks, and use IV iron from the second trimester for non-response, intolerance or late presentation.

sections.title: Define and screen
items: BSH: anaemia is Hb below 110 g/L in the first trimester, below 105 g/L in the second and third trimesters, and below 100 g/L postpartum. WHO 2024 uses below 110 g/L in the first and third trimesters and below 105 g/L in the second; ACOG and CDC use 11.0, 10.5 and 11.0 g/dL.
Check a full blood count at booking and at 28 weeks (BSH); ACOG screens in the first trimester and again at 24 to 28 weeks.
Iron deficiency is by far the commonest cause. Also consider folate or B12 deficiency, haemoglobinopathy (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease), malaria, hookworm, chronic disease, and blood loss.

Risk factors for iron depletion: previous anaemia, multiparity, pregnancy within a year of a previous birth, multiple pregnancy, teenage pregnancy, vegetarian or low-iron diet, recent bleeding or high bleeding risk, and women who decline blood products.
Symptoms or signs of decompensation at any Hb (breathlessness at rest, tachycardia, chest pain, heart failure) need urgent hospital assessment.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Serum ferritin below 30 micrograms/L confirms iron deficiency in pregnancy; ferritin can be falsely normal with inflammation or infection.
BSH: in normocytic or microcytic anaemia, a trial of oral iron is the first-line diagnostic test; a rise in Hb by 2 to 3 weeks confirms iron deficiency.
Know the haemoglobinopathy screening result; in women with a known haemoglobinopathy, check ferritin before giving iron and give iron only if ferritin is below 30 micrograms/L.
No response despite adherence and correct use: check ferritin, folate, B12, haemoglobinopathy status, and look for malabsorption or blood loss; consider malaria and hookworm in endemic areas.

sections.title: Prevention for all pregnant women
items: WHO 2016: daily oral iron 30 to 60 mg elemental iron plus 400 micrograms folic acid throughout pregnancy; prefer 60 mg where 40% or more of pregnant women are anaemic.
WHO alternative where anaemia prevalence is below 20% or daily iron is not tolerated: 120 mg elemental iron plus 2.8 mg folic acid once weekly (confirm Hb is normal first).
BSH: offer non-anaemic women at increased risk of iron depletion empirical oral iron, or check ferritin and offer iron if it is below 30 micrograms/L.
Folic acid 400 micrograms daily from before conception to 12 weeks; higher doses for women at high risk of neural tube defects per local policy.
Dietary advice on iron-rich foods and on taking iron away from tea, coffee, calcium and antacids.

sections.title: Oral iron
items: BSH: start treatment within 2 weeks of identifying anaemia with a ferrous salt giving 40 to 80 mg elemental iron every morning or on alternate mornings. Alternate-day dosing may improve absorption and tolerance (BSH, ACOG).
Take on an empty stomach with water or a vitamin C source, at least 1 hour before food, drinks or other medicines including multivitamins and antacids.
WHO: if anaemia is diagnosed, give 120 mg elemental iron plus 400 micrograms folic acid daily until Hb reaches 110 g/L, then return to the preventive dose.
Recheck Hb at 2 to 3 weeks to confirm adherence, correct use and response. Poor response: check adherence and look for other causes (folate deficiency, malabsorption, haemoglobinopathy).
Once Hb is normal, continue iron for about 3 months and until at least 6 weeks after birth to replenish stores.

sections.title: Intravenous iron
items: BSH: offer IV iron from the second trimester to women with confirmed iron deficiency who do not respond to or cannot tolerate oral iron, and to those with Hb below 100 g/L after 34 weeks. Avoid IV iron in the first trimester.
ACOG: consider IV iron when oral iron is not tolerated or fails, or when rapid repletion is needed late in pregnancy.
Calculate the dose from weight and Hb deficit; modern preparations allow total replacement in 1 or 2 infusions (ferric carboxymaltose or ferric derisomaltose) or several smaller doses (iron sucrose).

Give only where anaphylaxis can be treated, with observation during and after the infusion; check the cannula first to avoid skin staining. Do not give with active infection or in anaemia not due to iron deficiency.
Ferric carboxymaltose can cause hypophosphataemia; check phosphate if repeated doses are given or symptoms suggest it.

sections.title: Severe anaemia, birth and transfusion
items: Refer to secondary care for severe anaemia (Hb below 70 g/L), significant symptoms, advanced gestation (over 34 weeks) or failure to respond to oral iron.

Reserve red cell transfusion for active or anticipated major bleeding, imminent cardiac compromise or symptoms needing immediate correction, not for Hb alone; transfuse single units with reassessment.
Plan birth in hospital for women still anaemic near term: IV access, group and screen, active management of the third stage and early treatment of postpartum haemorrhage.
After birth, check Hb within 48 hours if blood loss exceeded 500 mL, anaemia was not corrected antenatally, or there are symptoms of anaemia.

Postpartum Hb below 100 g/L in a stable woman: oral elemental iron 40 to 80 mg daily for at least 3 months; IV iron if oral iron previously failed or was not tolerated, or if symptoms need prompt correction (BSH).

sections.title: Special situations
items: Haemoglobinopathy carriers (thalassaemia trait) may still become iron deficient: give iron only when ferritin confirms deficiency, and offer partner testing and specialist review.
Vegetarian and vegan women, multiple pregnancy and short interpregnancy intervals: lower threshold for ferritin testing and empirical iron.

India: Anaemia Mukt Bharat gives IFA (60 mg iron plus 500 micrograms folic acid) daily from the second trimester, 2 tablets daily for mild to moderate anaemia, IV iron up to 34 weeks for Hb 5 to 6.9 g/dL, and transfusion for Hb below 5 g/dL; follow the national programme where it applies.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Not rechecking Hb after 2 to 3 weeks, so ineffective oral iron continues until late pregnancy.
Giving oral iron with meals, tea, calcium or antacids, or in divided doses several times a day, which worsens absorption and side effects.
IV iron in the first trimester or for anaemia not caused by iron deficiency.
Transfusing a stable woman on the basis of Hb alone, or transfusing rapidly in severe chronic anaemia and causing pulmonary oedema.

drugs.name: Oral iron (ferrous salt)
drugs.dose: Treatment 40 to 80 mg elemental iron orally once each morning or on alternate mornings (BSH); WHO 120 mg elemental iron daily with 400 micrograms folic acid until Hb 110 g/L
drugs.notes: Empty stomach with water or vitamin C. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg gives about 65 mg elemental iron. Constipation and nausea are common.

drugs.name: Iron and folic acid (prevention)
drugs.dose: 30 to 60 mg elemental iron plus 400 micrograms folic acid orally daily throughout pregnancy (WHO); or 120 mg iron plus 2.8 mg folic acid once weekly where appropriate
drugs.notes: 60 mg daily preferred where anaemia prevalence is 40% or more.

drugs.name: Folic acid
drugs.dose: 400 micrograms orally daily from preconception to 12 weeks
drugs.notes: Higher doses for women at high risk of neural tube defects per local policy.

drugs.name: Ferric carboxymaltose
drugs.dose: 20 mg/kg IV, maximum 1000 mg per single infusion, over at least 15 minutes; total dose from weight and Hb deficit
drugs.notes: Second or third trimester or postpartum. Can cause hypophosphataemia.

drugs.name: Ferric derisomaltose
drugs.dose: 20 mg/kg IV as a single infusion, total dose from weight and Hb deficit
drugs.notes: Second or third trimester or postpartum. Observe for hypersensitivity.

drugs.name: Iron sucrose
drugs.dose: 200 mg IV per dose, repeated up to 3 times a week until the calculated total dose is given
drugs.notes: Requires several visits; useful where single-dose products are unavailable.

drugs.name: Packed red cells
drugs.dose: One unit at a time with clinical reassessment between units
drugs.notes: Active or anticipated major bleeding, imminent cardiac compromise or symptoms needing immediate correction.
